task: Write one sentence of your own using the word bourgeois. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know bourgeois should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In the port city's old quarter, the tall brick houses were built by the bourgeois of the spice trade — merchants rich enough for glass windows but never welcome at court.
The peasant stood on the old social ladder's lowest rung, working land he rarely owned; the bourgeois lived a full rung up, in town, with a shop or trade of his own.
The aristocrat looked down on the bourgeois from the ladder's top: whatever fortune a bourgeois piled up, he could not buy the birth and title the highest rung required.

A burgher is the bourgeois's near-twin in the Dutch and German towns: a town citizen of means, with a workshop, warehouse, or trade behind his name. Same rank, different map — and where bourgeois later picked up a sneer, burgher has stayed a plain historical label.

A townsman is anyone who lives in a town — the word records where he sleeps, not what he owns. A bourgeois is a particular kind of townsman: one with property and a trade, a shop or workshop of his own. Every bourgeois is a townsman; a penniless renter is only a townsman.

A merchant lives by buying and selling — the word names his trade, not his rank. Bourgeois names the rank itself: the propertied town class a successful merchant belonged to, alongside master craftsmen and lawyers. A ruined merchant is still a merchant; he may no longer be a bourgeois.
